title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and the ADR (architecture decision record) process. It is intended as the canonical engineering reference for new and existing services, libraries, and runtime components.

Goals
- Provide a single source of truth for architecture-level constraints and best practices.
- Ensure consistent developer ergonomics and predictable operational behavior across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Reduce risk (security, reliability, performance regressions) by standardizing critical interfaces and SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to all services owned by Engineering: API endpoints (internal and external), backend services, model-serving runtime components, infra IaC, and observability instrumentation.
- Exceptions require an ADR and approval by the owning platform/infra and the service owner.

Principles (quick reference)
- Stable developer contracts: API backward compatibility for public routes, semantic versioning for internal libraries.
- Observable by default: every service emits metrics, traces, and sanitised structured logs.
- Performance-within-budget: services must meet defined P95/P99 latency SLOs and cost targets for expected request patterns.
- Security and least privilege: follow organization-wide RBAC and KMS usage for secrets.

1) API Standards
------------------
Intro: APIs are the durable contracts between clients and Redwood services. They must be documented, versioned, and designed for operational clarity.

Key requirements:
- Schema-first: public and cross-team APIs must publish an OpenAPI (v3) spec stored in the repo under /api/openapi.yaml and validated in CI.
- Versioning: use semantic versioning for major-breaking changes. Major version increments must be accompanied by a deprecation schedule (minimum 90 days) and a migration guide.
- Error model: standardized error envelope: { code, message, request_id, details? }. Map HTTP status codes consistently (400 for client errors, 401/403 auth, 404 not found, 429 throttling, 5xx server errors).
- Pagination: prefer cursor-based pagination for large result sets.
- Rate limiting: public endpoints must include a rate-limit header set: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

Example API checklist (to include in PR):
1. OpenAPI spec added/updated and CI passes.
2. Schema changes non-breaking or major versioned.
3. Contract tests added for consumers.
4. Integration test for expected SLO under load.

2) Coding Standards
--------------------
Languages in use: Go (backend services), Python (model utils, evals), TypeScript (console front-end), Rust (performance-critical runtime components).

General rules:
- Linting: repo-level linters enforced in CI (golangci-lint, ruff/flake8, eslint).
- Formatting: gofmt/gci, black/isort, prettier enforced.
- Testing: unit tests required; >60% coverage for critical libs; 80%+ desirable for platform libraries.
- PR checklist: clear description, linked Jira, tests, changelog entry for public APIs, performance impact statement if touching hot code paths.

Code review guidance:
- Prefer small focused PRs (< 300 LOC) and link design discussions.
- Reviewers must verify backward compatibility for exported types and APIs.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC & Cloud)
----------------------------------------
Ownership: eng-infra owns shared modules; individual teams own service stacks.

Standards:
- IaC: Terraform (>=1.5) is the standard. All modules must be published in the internal module registry. PRs that change shared modules require at least two approvers from eng-infra and the module owner.
- Environments: clear separation: prod, staging, dev. No cross-tenant credentials in code.
- Network: VPCs by environment. Private services default to internal subnets. Public ingress via shared ALB/API gateway with WAF policies applied.
- Secrets: use KMS + Secrets Manager; no plaintext secrets in repos.
- Capacity: GPU fleet changes require capacity planning doc and SRE signoff (see eng-sre/capacity-planning).

Example IaC table (required fields for a service module):
| field | description | example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| module_name | canonical registry path | registry/redwood/storage |
| owner | team/Slack handle | eng-serving-runtime |
| cloud_account | aws account id | 123456789012 |
| required_tags | cost center, team | team:eng-serving-runtime,env:prod |

4) Model-Serving Standards
---------------------------
Purpose: ensure models are served safely, consistently, and with predictable performance across hosted/dedicated/private modes.

Core rules:
- Model pinning: all serving configs must include a pinned model artifact version and checksum. Rolling to a new model requires a canary rollout and a model-eval against the golden prompt-set.
- Quantization/Profiles: maintain quantization profiles per model in /quantization-profiles. Profiles include supported dtypes (fp16, int8) and validated quality deltas.
- KV/Prefix cache: services that support KV caching must expose cache-hit metrics and provide fallback behavior on cache failure.
- Batching: recommended default: adaptive batching with SLO-aware batching thresholds. Batching configs must expose max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, and batching_strategy.
- Fallbacks: policy must define fallback model variants (cost-tier and capability-tier) and auto-fallback conditions (queue-depth, latency breach, OOM).

Example minimal serving config snippet (in YAML, for reference):
```
model: redwood/llama-large:2026-02-01
quantization_profile: llama-large-int8
max_batch_size: 32
max_wait_ms: 12
fallbacks:
  - model: redwood/llama-medium:2025-11-10
    condition: p95_latency > 600ms
```

5) Observability Standards
--------------------------
Goal: make debugging and reliability analysis fast and consistent.

Metrics (must emit):
- Request level: requests_total, requests_success_total, requests_error_total, requests_latency_seconds_bucket (histogram).
- Model-serving: tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hits_total, kv_cache_misses_total, batch_size_distribution.
- System: cpu_utilization, gpu_utilization, memory_usage_bytes, queue_depth.

Tracing/logging:
- Traces: instrument request entrypoint to emit a trace ID propagated through services. Use OpenTelemetry.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, instance_id, request_id/trace_id, user_id (if present), message, error_details. Logs should avoid PII; sensitive fields must be redacted by sanitizer middleware.

SLOs and Alerts:
- Service SLOs: default SLO is 99.9% availability and P95 latency target defined per service (example: API gateway P95 < 120ms, model-runtime P95 < 200ms).
- Error budget policy: when an SLO breach consumes >50% of monthly error budget, trigger an incident review and slowdown of risky rollouts.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarking
--------------------------------------
Performance expectations are differentiated by surface area (API, runtime, model-serving).

Benchmarks:
- Synthetic benchmarks: all model runtime changes must run the internal benchmarking suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) and publish results including throughput (tokens/s), median latency, P95/P99, memory and peak GPU utilization.
- Service-level load tests: load tests should be run against staging with representative dataset and workload profiles before major releases.

Thresholds (examples):
- API gateway: P95 < 120ms, P99 < 400ms for baseline text generation requests.
- Model runtime: P95 per-token latency < 5ms on target hardware for our quantized small models (depending on hardware class).

Perf regression process:
1. Detect regression via perf monitoring or PR benchmark.
2. Open an ADR when the regression is due to architectural or non-trivial design change.
3. If urgent, revert the change and open a postmortem.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
--------------------------------------------
Purpose: capture durable architectural decisions and tradeoffs. ADRs are required for any deviation from the standards above or for major architecture changes.

Template (store ADRs under docs/adr/ in the repo):
- ADR-<NNN>-short-title.md
- Fields: title, status (proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded), context, decision, consequences, owners, date.

Lifecycle:
1. Draft ADR and discuss in architecture review channel.
2. Add reviewers: at a minimum include the owning platform team and eng-infra or eng-serving-runtime depending on scope.
3. Accept ADR via documented approvals (two approvers including one platform/infra).
4. Implement and reference ADR in changelog; update related docs.

Example decisions that require an ADR:
- Switching the canonical model serialization format.
- Introducing a new network topology that alters ingress/egress patterns.
- De-commissioning a global observability pipeline.

8) Ownership, Onboarding & Enforcement
--------------------------------------
- Each service must declare an owner in service manifest (owner: team-slack-handle) and a primary and secondary oncall in the runbook.
- Compliance checks: CI includes linters, OpenAPI validation, IaC plan checks; a weekly policy job runs to detect drift (tagging, secrets in code, missing metrics).
- Exceptions: short-lived exceptions are permitted (max 14 days) and require an ADR if the exception becomes permanent.

9) Rollout & Change Management
-------------------------------
- Canary releases for model and config changes (minimum 5% traffic, 24 hours stable) before full rollouts.
- For infra upgrades (e.g., TF module change affecting prod), require a migration plan, canary, and SRE signoff.
- Major API changes require a public deprecation notice and migration helpers/client library updates.

- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture (traces and kernel selection docs)
